Structure 3 Classification of matter 
Organic compounds are all substances containing carbon atoms except elemental 
carbon, its oxides, carbonic acid, carbonates, carbides and cyanides. Carbon 
atoms readily form strong covalent bonds with one ancther, producing chains, 
branches and cycles. Organic compounds include fuels, solvents, drugs, plastics 
and various biological molecules, such as DNA, proteins, carbohydrates and fats. 
Formulas of organic compounds 
Carbon is a group 14 non-metal with four electrons in its outer energy level. 
In all organic compounds, carbon is tetravalent. The elemental composition 
of organic compounds is represented by empirical and molecular formulas, 
while the bonding order of atoms in molecules is shown by structural 
formulas (table 4). Three-dimensional shapes of molecules are represented by 
stereochemical formulas and 3D models. 
* Empirical formula shows the simplest integer ratio of atoms in a chemical substance. 
* Molecular formula shows the exact number of atoms of each kind in the molecule. 
* Full structural formula shows all atoms and all covalent bonds in the molecule. 
* Condensed structural formula shows all atoms but omits single covalent bonds, with all monovalent 
substituents grouped together. Double and triple bonds are shown optionally. 
» Skeletal formula shows all bonds between non-hydrogen atoms as lines but omits atom labels for carbon 
atoms and any hydrogen atoms attached to carbon atoms. 
* Stereochemical formula shows the 3D arrangement of atoms in a molecule, typically by using solid and 
hashed wedges.

Structure 3 Classification of matter 
Each type of formula has its purpose, advantages and disadvantages. 
Empirical and molecular formulas are useful in stoichiometric calculations, 
but they provide no information on the structure and shape of the 
molecules they represent. Full structural formulas show all bonds and 
atoms, which is important for calculations involving bond enthalpies 
(Reactivity 1.2), but take up extra space and require more time to draw, 
especially for large molecules. Similarly, stereochemical formulas provide 
information on the shapes of molecules and identity of stereocisomers at 
the expense of size and complexity. In contrast, skeletal formulas save 
space, but their interpretation requires experience and mental effort. 
Finally, 3D models focus our attention on the spatial arrangement of 
atoms in a molecule, but their construction requires modelling kits or 
computer software.

group(s) or, if such groups are absent, the largest number of consecutive compounds developed by

Structural isomers 
Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different order of 
atoms and/or bonds in their molecules. Structural isomers can belong to the 
same or different classes of organic compounds and thus might differ in both 
chemical and physical properties. 
Chain isomers, also known as skeletal isomers, differ in the configuration of their 
carbon backbone. For example, pentane (CsHu) has three skeletal isomers: 
n-pentane 2-methylbutane 2,2-dimethylpropane 
Position isomers have the same carbon backbone but different positions of a 
multiple bond or functional group. For example, butene (C4HB} and propanol 
(C,H,OH) have two position isomers each:

functional groups and thus belong to different classes of organic compounds. 
For example, the molecular formula C,H O can represent either an alcohol

Stereoisomers 
Sterecisomers are different molecules with the same composition and 
bond connectivity but different spatial arrangement of constituent atoms. 
Stereoisomers must not be confused with conformations, or conformers, which 
are different forms of the same molecule. Conformers cannot be isolated as 
individual compounds because they quickly interconvert by free rotation about 
a o (sigma) bond (figure 10, top). In contrast, stereoisomers can be isolated, as 
their interconversion would require breaking and reforming a @ or x (pi) bond 
(figure 10, bottom).

Enantiomers have identical physical properties except that they rotate the 
plane of polarized light in opposite directions by the same angle. However, 
a mixture containing equal amounts of two enantiomers is optically inactive, 
as the effects of individual enantiomers cancel each other. Such a mixture is 
known as a racemic mixture or racemate. The identity and purity of a chiral 
compound can be determined using a polarimeter. 
The chemical properties of enantiomers are identical in reactions with 
non-chiral compounds but differ when a chiral reactant or solvent is used. 
Chirality is particularly important in biology and medicine, where one of the 
enantiomers can be beneficial for the organism while the other can be toxic or 
responsible for unwanted side effects.

Mass spectrometry 
In a mass spectrometer (MS), the molecules of astudied compound are 
ionized, producing positively charged molecular ions. The mass-to-charge 
ratio (m/z) of the molecular ion corresponds to the relative molecular mass of 
the studied compound. 
Molecular ions often break up into pairs of fragments, typically a cation and 
aradical, but only cations are shown in mass spectra. The m/z ratios of the 
cations depend on the nature of the substituents and functional groups 
present in the original molecule. For example, ethanoic acid, CH,COOH

Combining analytical techniques 
To determine the structure of a molecule, you may need to interpret 
experimental data obtained by different analytical technigues, including IR and 
NMR spectroscepy, mass spectrometry and combustion (elemental) analysis. 
In most cases, you can use the strategy outlined below. 
* Determine the empirical formula of the analysed compound using the 
combustion analysis data, as outlined in example 10 from Structure 1.4. 
* |dentify the molecular ion peak in the MS spectrum and compare its m/z 
ratio with the M value for the empirical formula to determine the molecular 
formula. 
* Determine the total number of multiple bonds and/or rings in the molecule 
by comparing its molecular formula with that of a corresponding alkane. 
* |dentify the chemical bonds and functional groups that might be presentin 
the molecule using its IR spectrum and molecular formula. 
* Determine the number of different chemical environments of hydrogen 
atoms in the molecule from the number of signals in its NMR spectrum. 
* Identify hydrocarbon fragments (CH, CH, and CH,) and functional groups 
in the molecule using the integration trace in the NMR spectrum. 
Write down all deduced molecular fragments and link them together to 
match the splitting patterns of signals in the NMR spectrum. 
Double-check that your proposed structure matches all spectroscopic and 
analytical data. 
This strategy is not exhaustive. The steps listed above can be reordered or 
skipped, depending on the available data and your personal preferences. In 
particular, the first two steps are not required if you already know the molecular 
formula. The functional groupl(s) in the molecule can be deduced from its 
reactivity. However, you must always make sure that your final answer does not 
contradict any analytical data given in the question.

Thermochemistry studies temperature changes and heat transfer during 
chemical or physical processes. At constant pressure, the amount of heat 
released or absorbed in a chemical reaction or change of state is equal to the 
enthalpy change, AH, of that reaction or change of state. 
The first law of thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or 
destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another. A specific 
physical or chemical change will always absorb or release the same amount of 
energy when it is carried out under the same conditions. This energy can be 
determined by measuring the amount of heat transferred between the system 
and the surroundings.

specific heat capacity (¢) of water is approximately ten times higher than that 
of copper (table 1). In the general case, the amount of heat (Q) transferred to 
the sample and the temperature change (AT) of that sample are related as
